name: Time value equals opportunity cost determined by skill count
definition: Time is universal but its value is not. The value of an hour equals the opportunity cost of what you could productively do in that hour. More skills create more productive options per hour, which increases opportunity cost, which makes time feel more scarce and valuable. Someone with no skills to fill time productively has low opportunity cost and therefore low time value.
core_claim: If you acquire more skills, then each hour of time becomes more valuable to you, because more skills create more productive options per hour, increasing opportunity cost. Someone 'just waiting' has low time value because they have nothing productive to fill those hours with.

idea_origin.event_summary: Previously didn't understand why code J valued his time so much and seemed like 'such a dick' about it. Alina said 'he likes you, he spends time with you' and speaker thought 'that's the minimum amount of importance you could give someone.'
idea_origin.trigger: Realizing that with more skills, two hours of playing video games or talking to friends now represents real opportunity cost—could be learning to trade, building bots, improving content systems. This wasn't true before having those skills.
idea_origin.lesson_learned: Time is universal but doesn't cost the same to everybody. The difference is the opportunity cost that unit of time takes away from them, which is determined by the skills they have to fill it productively.

canonical_instruction: Identify the user's current skill count and list what productive activities they could do in a given time block. Compare this to someone with fewer skills who would have fewer options. Calculate the implicit opportunity cost difference. Show that more skills = more options = higher opportunity cost = time feels more scarce. If user has low skill count, note that acquiring skills will automatically increase their time value.

audiences: people wondering why successful people guard their time
people who feel time-rich but skill-poor
situations: deciding whether to spend time on leisure vs skill-building
understanding why someone values their time more than you do
justifying investment in learning new skills
exclusions: situations where rest/leisure is the productive choice
contexts where skill count is fixed (e.g., highly specialized roles)

transformation_rules: List the user's current skills that could productively fill time
For each hour in question, list 2-3 productive alternatives they're giving up
Compare to someone with fewer skills (what would they be doing? 'just waiting')
Name the opportunity cost explicitly in terms of outcomes (money, learning, progress)
Show that acquiring more skills will automatically increase future time value
tests: Output lists specific skills and specific productive alternatives (not vague 'could be productive')
Output includes a contrast between high-skill and low-skill time value
No generic 'time is valuable' advice without naming the mechanism (skill count)
Output references concrete examples like learning trading, building bots, or similar skill-specific activities
counterexamples: Situations where rest genuinely is the highest-value use of time (recovery, avoiding burnout)
People who have maximized skill count in their domain and need depth not breadth
Contexts where time value is externally set (hourly wage with no alternatives)
input_triggers: wondering why successful people guard their time
feeling like you have 'too much time' and nothing to do
friend who is 'just waiting' instead of being proactive
not understanding why someone else values their time more than you
two hours feels like nothing to you but everything to someone else
realizing you could be doing X, Y, or Z right now instead

related.note: Skill transference increases skill count, which increases time value via this principle

components.name: Time is universal but value is not
components.applies_when: Comparing time value across people with different skill levels

components.name: Skills create productive options to fill time
components.applies_when: User has skills that could productively fill a given time block

components.name: Opportunity cost determines subjective time value
components.applies_when: Calculating what is given up by spending time on activity X instead of Y

components.name: Low skill count means 'just waiting' with no opportunity cost
components.applies_when: Someone has few skills and therefore few productive alternatives (like Joey waiting for interview)
